analysis.one_liner: Opens the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain to oil and gas drilling.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referral, dying without a vote or cosponsors in the 109th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the legal ban on oil and gas drilling in the coastal plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, open roughly 1.5 million acres to competitive leasing, and write rules that steer review away from alternatives and toward quick lease sales. It also grants land to Alaska Native corporations, waives some federal land-use rules, narrows court review, and caps a small aid fund for local communities at $10 million.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies that would gain access to new federal acreage for exploration and production, and Alaska Native corporations receiving land conveyances.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the statutory prohibition (Section 1003 of ANILCA) that currently bars oil and gas production in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge [S2][S3].
Directs the Interior Secretary to run a competitive leasing program with a first lease sale within 22 months and at least 200,000 acres of high-potential tracts [S2][S3].
Conveys land to the Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation and Arctic Slope Regional Corporation, and creates a local impact aid fund capped at $10 million [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the loss of a wilderness resource permanently, and any environmental damage to caribou habitat and subsistence lands is not recoverable if drilling proceeds.

drawbacks.text: Requires the Secretary to analyze only one leasing alternative, with no study of non-leasing options, and presumes the government's environmental analysis is correct [S2][S3].
Limits all legal challenges to the D.C. Circuit on a 90-day deadline, restricting the ability of citizens or conservation groups to contest decisions [S2][S3].
Caps the local impact aid fund at $10 million despite authorizing $5 million per year, leaving communities little support for costs from drilling [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers new leasing opportunities for energy companies while waiving or limiting environmental review and public recourse; the costs fall on the refuge and the public's ability to challenge those decisions.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to committee, which never acted, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced in the House on January 4, 2005, and referred to the House Committee on Resources [S5].
No further action was taken and no cosponsors signed on before the 109th Congress ended [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died in committee, the statutory drilling ban stayed in place and the refuge's coastal plain remained closed to leasing for the rest of the Congress.

for.name: Don Young
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to open the ANWR coastal plain to leasing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill attracted no cosponsors and no recorded votes, leaving its level of support unclear.

industries.note: The bill would hand drillers access to roughly 1.5 million acres of the Arctic Refuge coastal plain through competitive leasing [S3]. The public would receive royalties of at least 12.5 percent on production, but the biggest value from opening the refuge flows to leaseholders [S3].
The bill conveys surface and subsurface land to Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation and Arctic Slope Regional Corporation and funds a small local impact aid program [S3].
